title: Dharma Position
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of understanding "Dharma position," which refers to the unique, non-dual nature of each moment in time. By recognizing that all moments are interconnected and empty of separate past, present, and future, we can respond more fully to reality without being limited by our thoughts about time. This perspective encourages us to accept reality as it is, without trying to grasp or manipulate it, allowing for a deeper understanding of the present moment.

sentences.text: My chi sha was a slacker today and didn't get me any water.
I'm going to begin and end our talk today with brief readings of Uchi.
Uchi will not be the theme of the talk, mostly because I totally do not feel qualified to speak about Uchi from this seat.
An ancient Buddha, Yaoshan, said:
*For the time being, stand on top of the highest peak.
For the time being, proceed along the bottom of the deepest ocean.
For the time being, three heads and eight arms of a fighting demon.
For the time being, an eight or sixteen foot body of a Buddha.
For the time being, a staff or a whisk.
For the time being, a pillar or a lantern.
For the time being, the children of common families, shang and li.
For the time being, the earth and sky.
For the time being here means time itself is being, and all being is time.
The golden sixteen foot body is time.
Because it is time, there is the radiant illumination of time.
Study it as the twelve hours of the present.
Three heads and eight arms is time.
Because it is time, it is not separate from the twelve hours of the present.*
So this is the beginning of Uchi.
What I'm going to talk about today does have a little bit to do with Uchi, because it is a phrase I came across while studying Uchi.
The phrase is Dharma position, and it has to do with time.
It has to do with non-duality, and it has to do with our meditation.
I also stumbled across another Dogen poem called The Prescription for Meditation, from his Chinese poem series.
*Dynamic functioning is the essence of all Buddhas.
Functioning dynamism is the essence of all patriarchs.
Spontaneously disclosed without thinking, fully manifested without obstruction.
Spontaneously disclosed without thinking, its spontaneous disclosure is in and of itself fully revealed.
Fully manifested without obstruction, its full manifestation is in and of itself completely realized.
The spontaneous disclosure fully revealed in and of itself is completely attained without defilement.
The full manifestation completely realized in and of itself is completely attained without leaning straight or bent.
Complete attainment is revealed in and of itself without defilement.
Full manifestation is realized in and of itself without loss or lack.
Complete realization is attained in and of itself without leaning straight or bent.
Realization is exerted in and of itself without design.
The water is clear to the very bottom.
Fish swim just like fish.
The vast sky is empty up to the firmament.
Birds fly just like birds.*
So, good morning.
I really do hope that it is a good morning for you.
I wish you well.
I sincerely wish you health and contentment.
I appreciate that you are spending part of your Memorial Day here with us, meditating and considering the Dharma.
Those of us who can get vaccinated probably have had an opportunity to get our shots by now.
We can go freely to see friends and family again.
I myself am looking forward to visiting my family in Germany this coming August, I hope.
The weather in the Pacific Northwest is at its most gorgeous.
Many of us are looking forward to hitting the road and traveling.
Several national parks already require reservations to avoid total chaos and mayhem.
The number of visitors they allow is already mind-boggling, and I really understand it.
Many of us have dealt with some form of cabin fever at one time or another during the last 15 months.
But let's not drop our guard too much.
Let us be careful for the sake of all beings.
Anti-vaccination and anti-science movements appear to gather strength, and COVID-19 and its variants will remain with us for a long time, it seems.
It seems that the virus will not respect the views of people who are not believing in what science finds.
I almost said COVID-19 will be with us permanently, but I caught myself in time.
So yes.
Let's go out and enjoy our ability to be more social, to meet in person and not by screen.
To have a meal with friends, visiting favorite haunts and exploring new sites.
Keeping all this in mind, Red Cedar has decided to suspend the Zen Life events during summer.
So this is the second to last talk.
Next Sunday, Tim will give the final talk, and then we will break for summer.
In mid-September, we will resume, hopefully re-energized with fresh views.
I do hope that we will all meet again in full health.
Maybe in September, we might be able to resume Zazen in person again.
Tim is exploring some possibility.
And unless something really unexpected happens, Samish sesshin 2022 will actually happen at Samish again.
So I feel a little bit sentimental about this break.
Yes, I look forward to it, and I also will miss all the fantastic speakers we've had during the series.
I'm really grateful to them all.
I'm also really grateful to my partner, Reg, who played with his keys on the way out, and who's never complained that I turned the living room into a little Zen temple every Sunday.
And special thanks to Desiree, who has been such a great dohan.
And Talus, who's been the resident tech wizard and who's been recording the talks.
If it was up to me, it would probably be a real mess.
So thank you very much to you.
Like I said before, I'm especially grateful to the Dharma teachers who shared their understanding and wisdom with us.
And the greatest thank you is to you, who actually showed up and listened and thereby really made it possible.
And dear Zoom, thank you for being there and being available.
I apologize for not loving you as much as you deserve.
Many thank yous to the whole world.
I'm now changing tracks.
Today I would like to talk about a phrase I encountered a few months ago in Shinjuu Robert's book, Being Time, which is a commentary on Dogen's fascicle Uchi, The Time Being.
This is the book.
It is really quite wonderful, and I appreciate the care and attention that has gone into the writing of it.
I've probably heard that phrase before, but I didn't pay attention to it at the time.
The phrase is Dharma position, and it expresses unique particular moments, things or events.
This is what caught my attention in Shinjuu Robert's book:
*A Dharma position understood as a unique, independent moment has multiple aspects, which when taken together are being time.
Without understanding the nature of a Dharma position as a being time and all being time, we mistakenly experience unique particular moments*
like the Buddhist parable of the blind man examining the elephant.
I trust that you probably know the story of the blind men who are led up to an elephant, and each one of them touches a part and then argues that understanding.
The one touching the foot thought of the elephant as a pillar.
The one touching the tusk was sure that elephants are like the blade of a plow.
"Oh no, it is like a rope," said the man who held on to the tail.
"Oh no, it's like the thick branch of a tree," said the man who touched the trunk of the elephant.
"Ah, it is like a big fan," said the man who touched the ear.
"What are you saying?
It is like a huge wall," said the man who touched the side of the elephant.
Shinjuu Robert continues:

*Since nothing ever stays the same and all things are in flux due to their interactive, interpenetrating nature, it would be folly to say that a dharma position or moment of being time begins here and ends there.*
I'll skip a few lines.

*Now, although Dogen does not deny the conventional everyday sense of time as a horizontal timeline of sequential events that we experience as past, present and future, Dogen is concerned with the non-dual nature of time and being expressed in the present moment.
From the point of view of practice, a linear view of time can impede realization.*
End quote.
I was fascinated by investigating time from the standpoint of non-duality.

In my conventional thinking, it's so clear: this is the past, this is the present right now, and then the future is unknown, even though we may have plans and aspirations and thoughts about what the future will look like.
Of course, we shouldn't forget what happened in the past, and we see that the future lies in front of us.
And just this, this very moment where we breathe and touch and experience.
Yet our past, present and future, and our thoughts about past, present and future, do not obstruct our responding to reality.
Seen differently, this awareness is what allows us to choose.
It creates the space in which we decide how to go forward, the space in which we decide how to respond.
This is very different from being stuck in a rut, from mindless knee-jerk reaction.
So this is the independent nature of the Dharma position.
How come I overlooked that for such a long time?
Many Dharma teachers have talked about it.
I especially like Kastanahashi's definition: the unique non-repeatable stage of a thing's existence at any given moment.
It literally means position of one time, which might make us think that he says, "Well, this Dharma position is just this very thing at this moment, different from what it is in past and future."
But he continues: the Dharma position or state of being itself at each moment carries entire time.
Another teacher, Uchiyama Roshi, towards the end of his life, wrote a poem titled Samadhi, Treasury of the Radiant Light:
*Though poor, never poor, though sick, never sick, though aging, never aging, though dying, never dying.
Reality prior to division, here lies unlimited depth.*
I believe this is Uchiyama Roshi talking about Dharma position.
Seen one way, we are particular, limited beings in our karmic place with our gender, age, health, and so on.
Seen in another way, we are just part of a dynamic total.
And I'm sorry, but I cannot remember where I found this quote:
*That experience of wholeness cannot be achieved by taking the familiar dualities of mind and body, self and world, and by effort fusing them into one.
We can only find ourselves there, as it were, by accident.*
I really like this one.
So what does it mean to us?
My understanding is that it means that we cannot think ourselves there, that we can't go to a class and when we get to the end, we find the recipe for awakening.
We can't work ourselves into that place.
However, it may be, and it may happen at any moment, sitting in zazen, walking along the water, or washing the dishes at home, that we can find ourselves there.

In my understanding, Dharma position respects the uniqueness and the individual characteristics of each thing, each person, each happening, while at the same time recognizing its inherent emptiness, which is the same for everything.
It is Sandokai, the merging of difference and unity.
Because there is interdependence, there is emptiness.
There can be change, there will be change, and there is space for possibility.
This is why form is emptiness and emptiness is form.
In one hand, the boundless nature of all things, of all time, seeing Buddha in everyone.
In the other hand, each thing and moment is singular and individual.
It is unique.
It has a particular function.
So the ideal in Zen is to be able to move freely between these two positions, these two perspectives.
Sometimes we talk about the relative and the absolute, or the literal and the absolute.
Maybe not you, but when I heard that in the beginning, I was so sure that the absolute must be so much better, and that's where I want to go.
That's what I wanted to get.
It's okay to let the thinking do its grasping.
"Oh, the absolute.
It must be so much better.
I really want it."
But this is what thinking does, and we don't need to believe it, and we don't need to follow it.
In truth, it is the movement, the energy between the two poles that makes it come alive.
Here is a last quote from Shinju Robert's book:
*From the perspective of non-duality, past, present and future are present in this moment.
Yet at the same time, each moment must have the freedom to express its individual flavor.
A Dharma position holds all being time, a being's time and time's being in this very moment.
This is the complete non-duality of things, existence and time.
A particular being time expresses two states.
First, there is the universal state of all being time.
This is the inclusive nature of everything taken as a whole.
Second, a being's time is a particular event, person or thing, which is expressed as an independent Dharma position.
Simultaneously, a Dharma position is both universal being time and particular being time.
Everything is present at the same time without hindering the universal and particular nature of each other.
This is also true of time's being.*
So what can we take away from this?
We cannot exclude anything because everything is right before us.
Accepting reality, things as they are, is based on knowing that just this, this very moment, this very thing includes all.
We cannot reject anything because it does not fit into our thoughts or desires or ideas.
If we project our likes and dislikes, we chase after or reject, our suffering begins.
Or maybe I should say it continues.
Dharma positions are impermanent and interconnecting.
We could even call Indra's net a Dharma position.
*The manner in which all Dharmas interpenetrate is like a net of jewels, extending into all directions, infinitely, without limit.
As for the imperial net of heavenly jewels, it is known as Indra's net.
Because of the clarity of the jewels, they are all reflected in and enter into each other.
Within each jewel simultaneously is reflected the whole net.
Ultimately, nothing comes or goes.*
We can pick one particular jewel and examine it closely, and this individual jewel can immediately reflect the image of every other jewel.
Indra's net is an interconnected network formed by relationships.
It views the universe as a web of connections and interdependencies.
At the same time, we can look closely and see the beauty of each individual jewel.
How spectacular it is.
I will end my talk with the ending of Uchi.
*The old masters have thus uttered these words.
But is there nothing further to say?
You should say, mind and words arriving partially are the time being.
Mind and words not arriving partially are the time being.
Further, you should examine the time being.
To have him raise the eyebrows and blink is half the time being.
To have him raise the eyebrows and blink is the time being missed.
Not to have him raise the eyebrows and blink is half the time being.
Not to have him raise the eyebrows and blink is the time being missed.
Thus, to study thoroughly, coming and going, to study thoroughly, arriving and beyond arriving, as the time being of this moment.*
Thank you very much for listening.
If you have any thoughts or comments about Dharma positions and time being, please speak.
